title: Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling to Predict Drug-Drug Interactions of Aficamten in the Chinese Population.
authors: Ziyang Wang; Xiaofei Wu; Ranran Jia; Hongyun Wang
abstract:
Aficamten is a next-generation cardiac myosin inhibitor (CMI) developed for the treatment of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM). Although extensive clinical pharmacology studies have been conducted in Caucasian populations, limited information is available regarding drug-drug interaction (DDI) risks in the Chinese population. Given the contribution of multiple cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes to aficamten metabolism and inter-ethnic differences in CYP-mediated metabolic capacity, it is important to characterize DDI risks and associated changes in aficamten exposure in Chinese subjects.
A whole-body physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model of aficamten was developed using clinical data from Caucasian subjects and extrapolated to the Chinese population. The PBPK model was subsequently applied to compare aficamten exposure between Chinese and Caucasian populations and to predict DDIs in Chinese subjects.
Ethnic sensitivity analysis indicated that the key PK parameters of aficamten (AUC0-∞, Cmax, and T1/2) were comparable between Caucasian and Chinese populations. Overall, the predicted DDI magnitudes in the Chinese population were generally consistent with the corresponding Caucasian DDI simulations. Specifically, the model predicted that co-administration with the broad-spectrum CYP inhibitors amiodarone and fluconazole increased the AUC0-∞ of aficamten by 1.43- and 2.27-fold, respectively, whereas the strong inducers carbamazepine and rifampicin decreased its exposure by 35% and 71%, respectively. Notably, under the simulated fluconazole or amiodarone co-administration scenarios, the predicted AUC0-∞ of CYP2D6 intermediate metabolizers (IMs) was 2.22-fold and 1.50-fold higher than that in CYP2D6 normal metabolizers (NMs), respectively.
The PBPK model predicted substantial changes in aficamten exposure with broad-spectrum CYP inhibitors (eg, amiodarone, fluconazole) and strong CYP inducers (eg, carbamazepine, rifampicin), and identified CYP2D6 IMs receiving fluconazole or amiodarone as potentially sensitive scenarios. These model-based findings provide quantitative information for DDI risk assessment in Chinese subjects but require clinical confirmation.

title: Evaluation of CardiaZn Pediatric Biodegradable Stent in a Long-Term Animal Model.
authors: Daniel S Levi; Larry Latson; William C Stoffregen; Martin Bocks; Nicholas K Sharawy; Tim Moran
journal: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions
abstract:
A survey of interventional pediatric cardiologists identified bioresorbable stents for aortic and pulmonary coarctations as the most needed device.
PediaStent developed the CardiaZn stent and conducted a 2.5-year GLP preclinical study to evaluate device safety, biocompatibility, and functional performance.
Twelve Yucatan (17-23 kg) mini swine received two CardiaZn stents in the aorta and one in the pulmonary artery with terminal assessments performed at 3, 28, 360, 540, 730, and 902 days. At 180 days, all remaining animals underwent catheterization, with an additional CardiaZn stent placed over a previous aortic stent in four subjects. All subjects received CT scans at 1 year.
There were no stent migrations, evidence of vessel injury, angiographic obstruction, or stent fragment embolization. From 180 to 360 days, the pulmonary artery, sub-renal, and supra-iliac aortic stents increased in diameter by 18%, 24%, and 28%, on average, respectively. Simultaneously, the pulmonary and sub-renal aortic stents elongated by an average of 40%. All CardiaZn stents explanted from 28 through 902 days were completely endothelialized. Histopathology displayed moderate remodeling of the tunica media without loss of structural integrity or extension into the adventitia. MicroCT analysis showed loss of mass and structural integrity secondary to degradation resulting in stent cell disconnection, allowing for vessel growth by 9-12 months.
The CardiaZn stent provided vascular support for up to 9 months before safely degrading to allow for vascular growth. A clinical trial is planned to confirm safety and efficacy in children.

title: Comparative Outcomes of Self-Expanding Versus Balloon-Expandable Valves in Severe Aortic Stenosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Ahmed Elazab; Ahmed Hamdy G Ali; Ahmed Elbataa; Ahmed Mansour; Noha Hammad; Amr Galal; Osama Ahmed Abdelaziz; Mohamed Saad Sayed; Mohamed Hamouda Elkasaby; Marwa Shaaban; Mohammed Sabri Hassanin; Ahella Ismail A Mousa; Islam Y Elgendy; Mo'ath Alharasees; Ahmed Aly; Adham Khaled Ahmad Alali; William H Frishman; Wilbert S Aronow
abstract: Abstract: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is an established treatment for severe aortic stenosis, with self-expanding valves (SEV) and balloon-expandable valves (BEV) representing the two major platforms. However, their comparative clinical and hemodynamic performance remains uncertain. We systematically searched four electronic databases through August 2026 for studies comparing SEV and BEV in patients undergoing TAVR. The primary outcomes were permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and change in mean pressure gradient (MPG), while secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), stroke, paravalvular leakage (PVL), heart failure hospitalization, coronary obstruction, and prosthesis-patient mismatch (PPM). Twenty-three studies involving 21,609 patients were included. Compared with BEV, SEV was associated with a significantly greater reduction in MPG (MD -4.48, 95% CI -5.29 to -3.67; P < 0.0001) and lower risks of moderate (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.42-0.75) and severe PPM (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.25-0.44). Conversely, SEV was associated with higher risks of PPI (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.14-1.72; P < 0.0001), moderate-to-severe PVL (RR 2.28, 95% CI 1.65-3.14; P < 0.0001), and a small but significant increase in all-cause mortality. No significant differences were observed in MACE, stroke, heart failure hospitalization, or coronary obstruction..

title: Genetic Insights Into Cardiomyopathy With Restrictive Phenotype: Implications for Diagnosis and Personalized Care.
authors: Nianwei Zhou; Yi Sun; Xuemei Wei; Wenwen Liang; Fangmin Meng; Zhengdan Ge; Minmin Sun; Xiaotong Cui; Shuning Zhang; Cuizhen Pan; Junbo Ge; Xianhong Shu
abstract:
Cardiomyopathy with a restrictive phenotype is uncommon, genetically heterogeneous, and difficult to distinguish from advanced hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy. We aimed primarily to determine the diagnostic yield and spectrum of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants among patients with an echocardiographically defined restrictive phenotype; genotype-imaging and survival comparisons were prespecified exploratory analyses.
We screened 568 patients with cardiomyopathy who underwent whole-exome sequencing and comprehensive echocardiography. Thirty-three met the operational definition of restrictive phenotype. Variants were classified. Genotype-imaging associations and survival were analyzed exploratorily.
Among the 568 patients, 33 exhibited a restrictive phenotype: 7 had restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM), 20 had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a restrictive phenotype (HRCM), and 6 had dilated cardiomyopathy with a restrictive phenotype (HDRCM). Variant carriers had a smaller aortic sinus diameter. In addition, MYBPC3 variant carriers had greater ventricular wall thickness and more frequent septal hypertrophy. Both the HRCM and HDRCM groups showed hypertrophic features, with interventricular septal hypertrophy occurring more frequently in the HDRCM group. The estimated 5-year survival was 54.5%, and survival did not differ significantly according to genetic-variant status.
Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were frequent in this single-center cohort with restrictive physiology and were associated with selected imaging features. These exploratory findings support integrated genetic and echocardiographic evaluation.

title: Latest findings on complications following trans- catheter aortic valve replacement: A literature review.
authors: Masoud Rezaei; Davood Hekmatpou; Mohammad Abbasi; Ahmad Reza Baghernezhad; Niloofar Ahmadi
journal: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
abstract:
Severe aortic stenosis (As) is the most common valvular heart disease in developed countries, and transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has expanded across surgical risk groups. However, procedure-related complications remain clinically important, and their reported incidence and management have evolved with newer-generation devices and techniques. This review summarizes major TAVR complications, including their incidence and pathophysiology, risk factors, clinical impact, prevention and management, and outlines remaining knowledge gaps.
A structured narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted for studies published between 2012 and 2026, including randomized trials, registries, cohort studies, and systematic reviews.
Major complications reviewed included Stroke, Delirium, Conduction disturbances (CD) and Arrhythmias, Bleeding/Vascular(access) site injuries/Paravalvular leak (PVL), Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), Structural valve degeneration and thrombosis, Infective Endocarditis (IE) and Coronary Obstruction (CO).
TAVR complications remain multifactorial, and their incidence and management continue to shift with device evolution and procedural experience. Optimized patient selection, procedural refinement, frailty assessment, and individualized antithrombotic strategies remain important areas for improving outcomes.

title: Parenteral Nutrition as a Strategic Therapeutic Option for Onco-Geriatric Rehabilitation After Total Gastrectomy and Anastomotic Stenosis Complicated by an Aorto-Esophageal Fistula: A Case Report.
authors: Houssam Eddine Belaid; João Gabriel De Carvalho; Mariangela Gagliano
abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: The nutritional management of onco-geriatric patients after a total gastrectomy remains a challenge, especially in the context of postoperative complications, such as stenosis of the esophagojejunal anastomosis, and in the presence of an aorto-esophageal fistula. Parenteral nutrition is a relevant therapeutic option to maintain nutritional support and enable rehabilitation when oral and enteral feeding are no longer feasible in this specific clinical context; Case Presentation: We report here the case of a 76-year-old patient who underwent a total gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma with several dilated and stented esophagojejunal anastomoses. During the first postoperative year, the nutritional adaptation facilitated rehabilitation and helped him recover well. However, the occurrence of an aorto-esophageal fistula and its treatment with thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) made oral and enteral feeding impossible. This was associated with persistent asthenia, physical deconditioning, sarcopenia, weight loss, exercise intolerance, and increased dependence for activities of daily living. Although parenteral nutrition allowed for nutritional stability and the beginning of rehabilitation, a suspected nosocomial infection involving the aortic endograft led to his death before his treatment was complete; Conclusions: This case highlights the relevance of parenteral nutrition as a therapeutic option to continue rehabilitation when enteral access is judged unacceptably risky. However, the risk of infectious complications in the context of malnutrition can compromise the prognosis, and any suspicion of infection involving prosthetic material should be documented microbiologically as completely as possible whenever compatible with the patient's care objectives. Onco-geriatric assessment to manage older patients with esophagogastric cancer is recommended.

title: Subaxial Vertebral Artery Entrapment by Thyroid Cartilage and C5: Why Radiologists Should Think Beyond Bow Hunter's Syndrome-A Case Report.
authors: Farnaz Delavari; Patrik Michel; Vincent Dunet; Guillaume Fahrni
abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: Bow Hunter's syndrome is an uncommon cause of vertebrobasilar insufficiency caused by dynamic vertebral artery narrowing during head rotation or extension. It is classically described at the atlantoaxial level, whereas subaxial compression is less recognised. Thyroid cartilage-related vertebral artery compression is particularly rare and may mimic vertebral artery dissection on static imaging. This case highlights the need to distinguish anatomical conflict from clinically causal haemodynamic compression. Case Presentation: A 51-year-old man with vascular risk factors and a well-anticoagulated mechanical aortic valve presented with three transient ischaemic attacks within two hours, including left-hand paraesthesia, right hemianopia, transient aphasia, and right-hand paraesthesia. Symptoms occurred spontaneously, without clear relation to head or neck movement or trauma. Doppler ultrasound showed normal carotid and vertebral flow. CT angiography demonstrated focal stenosis of the right vertebral artery at the V1-V2 junction caused by an osteocartilaginous "pincer" between the right thyroid cartilage ala and the C5 transverse process. The axial appearance mimicked vertebral artery dissection, but multiplanar CTA and contrast-enhanced MRA supported external indentation without mural haematoma, intimal flap, pseudoaneurysm, or double lumen. Perfusion CT showed no focal hypoperfusion, and diffusion-weighted MRI showed no acute infarct. Because symptoms were not positional and competing embolic risk factors were present, conservative management was chosen. Conclusions: Thyroid cartilage-related subaxial vertebral artery compression is a rare diagnostic pitfall. Static imaging may suggest dissection or Bow Hunter's syndrome, but causality should not be inferred without compatible symptoms, exclusion of alternative mechanisms, and, when needed, dynamic confirmation.

title: Critical Tracheal Compression by a Double Aortic Arch in a Young Infant: A Case Report.
authors: Kabelo Molatedi; Mikail Amod; Jeandre Kotze; Ambrosius Swartbooi
abstract: Double aortic arch is a congenital vascular anomaly in which persistence of both fourth aortic arches creates a complete vascular ring around the trachea and esophagus. Severe airway compromise in early infancy may be life-threatening and can mimic intrinsic congenital airway disease. We report a six-week-old female infant with progressive noisy breathing, stridor, and respiratory distress, particularly during crying, who experienced three near-arrest episodes. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated a complete vascular ring formed by a double aortic arch with an atretic left arch and severe focal tracheal compression. The narrowest tracheal diameter measured 1.7 mm across a 5.1-mm segment at the T1/T2 level, with associated posterior esophageal compression. The right common carotid and right subclavian arteries arose from the right arch, whereas the left vertebral, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries arose from the left arch. The infant underwent thoracotomy and release of the vascular ring. Respiratory distress and stridor improved markedly after surgery, and she was discharged breathing room air without stridor at rest and feeding well. The imaging findings and postoperative response supported extrinsic vascular compression rather than documented intrinsic congenital tracheal stenosis or a tracheal web. Recognition of the characteristic vascular anatomy is essential because double aortic arch, pulmonary artery sling, and intrinsic congenital tracheal stenosis have different anatomic substrates and surgical implications.

title: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation Followed by Lung Cancer Resection in an Older Patient: A Case Report.
authors: Leena Khan; Syed S Qadri
abstract: The individual incidences of lung cancer and cardiovascular disease in the elderly population mean that there is a strong likelihood of both occurring simultaneously. Common practice for severe aortic stenosis (AS) would be surgical aortic valve replacement (AVR), unless deemed high-risk for this surgical procedure. Age and lung cancer both increase a patient's surgical risk; hence, the less invasive transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) to manage valve disease ahead of lung resection for lung cancer is an acceptable alternative after assessing other factors such as procedural risk, comorbidities, and prognosis. We present the case of an 82-year-old female patient who underwent a TAVI seven months before lung resection for an incidental diagnosis of lung cancer with staging T1b N0 M0. Postoperatively, she was treated for atrial fibrillation and lung collapse, then discharged after resolution of these complications on the eighth day after surgery, and remained well at follow-up three months later. This case report explores a situation when this sequence of interventions was appropriate due to increased surgical risk in the elderly population.

title: Coral reef aorta demonstrated by serial computed tomography: a case report.
authors: Tsuneaki Kawashima; Masaki Harada
abstract:
Coral reef aorta (CRA) is a rare vascular disorder characterized by dense, protruding calcified plaques within the abdominal aorta, often resulting in ischaemic symptoms. Because of its rarity and atypical presentation, CRA is frequently diagnosed at an advanced stage.
A 50-year-old male smoker with hypertension and hyperlipidaemia presented with progressive lower extremity symptoms. Four years before presentation, he developed bilateral lower limb numbness and was diagnosed with lumbar disc herniation, which likely masked the underlying vascular disease. One year before presentation, he developed intermittent claudication after ∼10 min of walking, followed by severe bilateral rest pain 1 month before presentation. The ankle-brachial index (ABI) was markedly reduced to 0.49 bilaterally. Computed tomography (CT) revealed extensive calcified plaques causing near occlusion of the infrarenal abdominal aorta. Serial CT over 6 years demonstrated progressive intraluminal calcification, facilitating diagnosis and treatment planning. Open aortic graft replacement with inferior mesenteric artery reconstruction was performed. Postoperatively, symptoms resolved completely, and the ABI improved to 1.13 (right) and 1.19 (left). At 1-year follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic with the ABI of 1.07 bilaterally, and CT confirmed graft patency.
This case highlights the importance of considering CRA in patients with lower limb ischaemia, particularly when symptoms are initially attributed to non-vascular conditions. Serial CT is essential for detecting progression and enabling timely diagnosis. Open surgical intervention remains the most reliable treatment and can achieve excellent clinical outcomes in advanced disease.

title: A screening method for aortic valve disease based on spectral analysis of a single-channel electrocardiogram using machine learning algorithms.
authors: Natalia Kuznetsova; Daniil Zelenov; Aleksandra Bogdanova; Ines Dhif; Ekaterina Shobonova; Anna Alekseeva; Dinara Mesitskaya; Abram Syrkin; Roman Komarov; Philippe Kopylov; Petr Chomakhidze
abstract:
Given the high prevalence of aortic heart disease and the importance of early diagnosis, there is a need to develop a simple screening method to identify significant aortic heart disease based on available biosignals, one of which is a single-channel electrocardiogram (ECG).
We aimed to develop a machine learning algorithm for analyzing single-channel electrocardiograms to identify patients with moderate to severe aortic stenosis and regurgitation, as well as significant aortic valve disease.
Patients (n = 2,503) underwent echocardiographic examination and single-channel I-lead ECG recording using a portable electrocardiograph. Moderate to severe aortic stenosis on echocardiography was present in 62 (2.4%) patients, and moderate to severe aortic regurgitation was present in 157 (6.3%). Single-channel ECG analysis was performed using advanced signal processing and machine learning techniques.
Both models were evaluated under an identical 10-fold group cross-validation framework. For detecting moderate or severe aortic stenosis, diagnostic accuracy was 0.650 (Se 57.9%, Sp 65.0%) for Balanced Random Forest and 0.662 (Se 46.4%, Sp 66.5%) for XGBoost. For moderate or severe aortic regurgitation, accuracy was 0.726 (Se 60.5%, Sp 73.3%) for Balanced Random Forest and 0.712 (Se 61.7%, Sp 71.9%) for XGBoost. For significant aortic valve disease, accuracy was 0.724 (Se 61.1%, Sp 73.4%) for Balanced Random Forest and 0.691 (Se 67.8%, Sp 69.2%) for XGBoost.
The results indicate good diagnostic accuracy and potential applicability for screening for significant aortic heart disease using single-channel ECG parameters analyzed with modern signal processing and machine learning techniques.Clinical Trial Registration: https://clinicaltrial.gov/, identifier NCT07099417.

title: Long-term survival after transcatheter aortic valve implantation in nonagenarian patients: a multicenter real-world study.
authors: Gianluca Pagnoni; Marco Loffi; Dalia Caleffi; Susan Darroudi; Giuseppe Masaracchia; Benedetta Frassoni; Francesco Marangi; Sophia di Michele; Davide Gabbieri; Luciano Losi; Alberto Monello; Fabio Alfredo Sgura; Salvatore Arrotti; Rosario Rossi; Daniele Iaccarino; Marco Ruozzi; Vincenzo Guiducci; Filippo Luca Gurgoglione; Giorgio Benatti; Luigi Vignali; Giampaolo Niccoli; Giuseppe Boriani; Daniela Aschieri; Francesca Coppi
abstract:
The growing number of nonagenarian patients with severe aortic stenosis has increased interest in transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) in this population. However, data on long-term outcomes remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate long-term survival and procedural outcomes of TAVI in nonagenarians and to explore clinical factors associated with long-term mortality.
We conducted an ambispective multicenter observational cohort study including patients aged ≥90 years who underwent TAVI for severe aortic stenosis between 2013 and 2021 at six centers in the Emilia-Romagna region, Italy. Baseline and procedural data were collected retrospectively, while outcome ascertainment combined prospective follow-up contacts with retrospective verification of dates of death or last confirmed vital status. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and associations with mortality were examined using an exploratory Cox regression analysis.
A total of 60 nonagenarian patients (mean age 91 ± 1.5 years; 67% female) were included. Procedural success was achieved in 97% of cases. In-hospital mortality was 5%, and 30-day mortality was 8.3%. Over a mean observation period of 5.7 years from TAVI to death or the last confirmed vital-status assessment, the Kaplan-Meier estimated 5-year survival was 35%. In the exploratory multivariable analysis, male sex and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) were associated with higher long-term mortality.
In patients aged ≥90 years selected by the Heart Team for TAVI, the Kaplan-Meier estimated 5-year survival was 35%. The procedure demonstrated a high success rate and an acceptable safety profile. Male sex and COPD showed an exploratory association with worse prognosis. These findings suggest that TAVI may be a feasible option in carefully selected nonagenarians when guided by comprehensive clinical assessment and individualized decision-making.

title: Dual-guidewire technique with cerebral embolic protection for brachiocephalic trunk bifurcation stenosis: a case report.
authors: Yulan Gan; Guoyin Pang; Guofei Zhang; Jun Yang; Wenyou Wu; Zhifu Song
abstract:
Severe stenosis at the terminal bifurcation of the brachiocephalic trunk involving the origins of the right common carotid artery and the right subclavian artery is a rare and highly challenging lesion of the supra-aortic vessels. Endovascular intervention carries a high risk of embolization and difficulty in delivering large-diameter stents.
We report a 60-year-old male patient who presented with intermittent dizziness and asymmetric blood pressure in the upper limbs. Color Doppler ultrasound and head and neck CT angiography revealed severe stenosis at the terminal bifurcation of the brachiocephalic trunk (stenosis rate approximately 90%), with the lesion involving the origins of the right common carotid artery and the right subclavian artery, accompanied by right subclavian artery steal phenomenon. The patient underwent brachiocephalic trunk balloon angioplasty and stenting via a single femoral artery access. An embolic protection device was deployed in the C1 segment of the right internal carotid artery for distal cerebral protection. During delivery of the stent, the filter guidewire provided insufficient support; a second guidewire was added as a buddy wire to establish a dual-guidewire rail technique, facilitating successful stent placement. Debris was observed in the retrieved filter. Postoperatively, the severe stenosis was relieved and the steal phenomenon resolved. At 1.5 years of follow-up, the patient reported no recurrence of dizziness, and the inter-arm blood pressure difference remained within the normal range.
In this selected case with clear antegrade flow direction, a single-access, single-filter strategy appeared feasible and may offer a simplified alternative for similar anatomical presentations. However, further validation in larger case series is warranted. The application of dual-guidewire rail technique to overcome difficulties in large-diameter stent delivery during brachiocephalic trunk intervention has been rarely reported.

title: Early changes in CT-derived quantitative flow ratio after transcatheter aortic valve replacement: a serial coronary physiological assessment.
authors: Lieyou Li; Yonghui Yu; Xinjie Zeng; Lijun Luo; Zhongwei Shi; Linyan Chen; Feng Hu; Lin Fan
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is an established treatment for severe aortic valve stenosis, but its effects on coronary physiology remain incompletely understood. CT-derived quantitative flow ratio (CT-QFR) enables non-invasive assessment of coronary physiology. This study aimed to investigate the early changes in CT-QFR following TAVR.
This retrospective study included consecutive patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent coronary computed tomography angiography before and within 7 days after TAVR. CT-QFR was calculated for all analyzable coronary vessels. Longitudinal changes in CT-QFR were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models with patient identifier as a random effect.
A total of 109 patients (324 coronary vessels) were analyzed. Plaque volume, plaque burden, and minimal lumen diameter remained unchanged after TAVR, whereas transvalvular pressure gradients decreased significantly. Overall, CT-QFR increased modestly following TAVR (β=0.018, P < 0.001). Significant increases were observed in the left anterior descending and right coronary arteries, whereas no significant change was detected in the left circumflex artery. Vessels with baseline %DS ≥50% demonstrated greater CT-QFR increases than those with less severe stenosis (interaction β=0.104, P < 0.001). Likewise, vessels with baseline CT-QFR <0.80 showed significantly larger post-TAVR increases than vessels with baseline CT-QFR ≥0.80 (interaction β=0.117, P < 0.001).
TAVR was associated with modest early increases in CT-QFR, particularly in vessels with greater anatomical stenosis or baseline physiological impairment. These findings suggest that coronary physiological assessment in severe aortic stenosis may be influenced by valve intervention and should be interpreted cautiously during the peri-TAVR period.

title: Temporal changes in dilated ascending aorta after transfemoral TAVR: a comparative analysis of bicuspid and tricuspid aortic valves.
authors: Qichen Xu; Zheng Xu; Xiaofu Dai; Liangwan Chen; Zhiqin Lin
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) addresses valvular obstruction but leaves concomitant ascending aortic dilatation untreated. Whether bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) morphology inherently accelerates post-TAVR aortic expansion compared with tricuspid aortic valves (TAV) remains uncertain.
This retrospective cohort study included 189 older adults (BAV, n = 87; TAV, n = 102) with severe aortic stenosis and ascending aortic dilatation (≥4.5 cm) undergoing TAVR. Annualized aortic expansion rates were evaluated utilizing linear mixed-effects models derived from serial computed tomography angiography over a median 27.0-month follow-up.
No ascending aortic dissection, rupture, or elective aortic interventions occurred during follow-up. The adjusted annualized expansion rate at the mid-ascending aorta was low and comparable between the BAV and TAV cohorts (0.43 vs. 0.39 mm/year; interaction P = 0.364). Progression rates at the distal ascending aorta and sinuses of Valsalva similarly demonstrated no significant morphological differences. No patient exhibited rapid progression (>5 mm/year). Although moderate or greater paravalvular leakage occurred exclusively in BAV patients (4.8% vs. 0.0%; P = 0.043), its overall incidence was low (2.2%); however, the extremely small number of cases precluded a definitive statistical assessment of its impact on longitudinal aortic expansion.
In this selected cohort, dilated ascending aortas exhibited slow intermediate-term expansion following transfemoral TAVR utilizing self-expanding valves, with comparable rates between BAV and TAV morphologies. These findings suggest that conservative management of concomitant ascending aortic dilatation may be a reasonable strategy in older TAVR candidates during intermediate-term follow-up, provided that strict blood pressure control and rigorous imaging surveillance are maintained.

title: Mapping human genetic associations to drug targets in valvular heart disease: an integrative evidence synthesis.
authors: Sara Moura-Ferreira; Tuna Ustunkaya; Momina Siddiqui; Kishore Kukendrarajah; Floriaan Schmidt; Raheel Ahmed; Mohammed Khanji; Anwar Chahal; Jan Verwerft; Rui Providencia
abstract:
Valvular heart disease (VHD) lacks disease-modifying pharmacological therapies. Drug repurposing guided by human genetics may help identify therapeutic opportunities. We aimed to integrate human genetic associations, drug-target information, and clinical evidence to identify repurposing opportunities and prioritise potentially druggable targets across the VHD spectrum.
We retrieved VHD-associated genetic variants from the NHGRI-EBI Genome-Wide Association Studies Catalogue and Ensembl, interrogated annotated genes in the Open Targets Platform, and evaluated linked drugs through structured searches of MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251071741).
We identified 1464 genetic associations corresponding to 844 unique variants and 582 candidate genes. Of these genes, 431 had tractability information and 51 had linked compounds, comprising 388 distinct pharmacological agents, 273 in phase 3 or 4 of clinical development. Drug-linked targets were concentrated in aortic stenosis. Clinical evidence supported therapeutic potential for 14 drugs, with preclinical or mechanistic cardiovascular support for eight additional drugs and adverse cardiovascular signals for four. An exploratory evidence-weighted framework prioritised targets according to genetic-functional evidence, tissue and mechanistic context, and translational tractability.
This genetics-informed evidence synthesis identifies drug-repurposing opportunities and a substantial gap between genetically supported targets and available therapies. The findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework for mechanistic validation and future valve-focused studies.

title: Survival benefit in patients with native aortic regurgitation using a dedicated transcatherter valve vs non-dedicated transcatheter valves.
authors: Andrea Messori; Roberto Brunoro; Melania Rivano
journal: Cardiovascular revascularization medicine : including molecular interventions
abstract:
Until recently, no standard of care has been established for patients with symptomatic native aortic regurgitation (AR) who are unsuitable for surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has been explored in this setting using off-label, non-dedicated valves originally designed for aortic stenosis. The recent ALIGN-AR trial evaluated the Trilogy valve, a dedicated transcatheter device specifically designed for native AR.
We performed an indirect comparison between the overall survival (OS) reported for the Trilogy valve in ALIGN-AR and OS from seven single-arm studies using non-dedicated valves. Individual patient data were reconstructed from published Kaplan-Meier curves using the IPDfromKM method. To ensure homogeneity, the follow-up period for the survival analysis was truncated at 24 months. Survival was analyzed using both hazard ratios (HR) and restricted mean survival time (RMST).
The analysis included 492 patients treated with the Trilogy valve and 867 treated with non-dedicated valves. OS was significantly improved with the Trilogy valve (HR 0.399; 95% CI 0.275-0.578; p = 0.0000011). RMST at 12 months was 11.4 months for the Trilogy valve versus 10.4 months for non-dedicated valves, corresponding to an OS gain of 1.0 months (95% CI 0.72-1.32) over the first year.
In patients with native AR undergoing TAVI, use of the dedicated Trilogy valve was associated with a highly significant survival advantage compared with non-dedicated devices, corresponding to an approximate 1-month gain in OS during the first 12 months after implantation.

title: SGLT2 inhibitor therapy following aortic valve intervention for aortic stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of mortality, heart failure, rhythm, renal, and valve-related outcomes.
authors: Hamzah Pratama Megantara; Iwan Dakota; Taofan Taofan; Suci Indrian; Ruth Grace Aurora; Suko Adiarto
abstract:
Residual mortality and heart-failure events remain common after aortic valve intervention for severe aortic stenosis. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes in heart-failure, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease populations, but their role following transcatheter or surgical aortic valve intervention remains uncertain.
PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Cochrane Library, citation tracking, and manually identified eligible studies were screened through June 2026 for randomized and observational studies comparing SGLT2i with usual care or no SGLT2i after aortic valve intervention. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251059332). Eligible populations included TAVR, SAVR, and bioprosthetic aortic valve evidence where available. Adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) were pooled using random-effects models while non-HR estimates and non-comparable endpoints were summarized narratively.
Twelve eligible reports were included, comprising one randomized trial and 11 observational studies. Most time-to-event estimates were reported from TAVR cohorts; two SAVR-only studies and one mixed bioprosthetic AVR study added complementary surgical and valve-durability data. In the pooled time-to-event analysis, SGLT2i use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.60-0.79; I²=5%; p < 0.001). The study-defined composite clinical outcome was also lower (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53-0.89; I²=57%; p = 0.005), although component definitions differed across studies. Estimates for heart-failure hospitalization or exacerbation, atrial fibrillation, and acute kidney injury were not statistically significant.
SGLT2i use after aortic valve intervention was associated with lower all-cause mortality in pooled time-to-event analysis. SAVR data were clinically informative but were not sufficiently homogeneous for separate quantitative pooling. Findings for composite, heart-failure, rhythm, renal, and valve-related outcomes remain less certain. Dedicated randomized trials are needed to confirm whether the observed association reflects a treatment effect and to define patient selection, treatment timing, and peri-procedural safety.

title: Emergency Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation in Mixed Bicuspid Aortic Valve Disease With a Horizontal Aorta: Return of Spontaneous Circulation Only After Left Ventricular Unloading.
authors: Tommaso Simone; Greta Cattaneo; Luca Testa; Francesco Bedogni; Gaspare Cannone
abstract: A 74-year-old man with mixed bicuspid aortic valve disease, combining severe calcific stenosis with severe regurgitation, and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 26% presented in normotensive cardiogenic shock with anuria and an arterial lactate of 12 mmol/L. Computed tomography showed a fibrocalcific left-right raphe and an aortic angulation of 66 degrees. Emergency transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve implantation was undertaken. The delivery system could not be advanced across the aortic arch despite escalation of guidewire support, and ventricular fibrillation degenerated into pulseless electrical activity refractory to resuscitation. Peripheral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was established, after which a 29 mm self-expanding prosthesis was implanted with an acceptable haemodynamic result and patent coronary ostia. Pulseless electrical activity nonetheless persisted. Return of spontaneous circulation followed only after a microaxial pump was advanced retrogradely across the freshly deployed prosthesis under fluoroscopic guidance alone, establishing an ECMELLA configuration. The patient died of multiorgan failure two days later. This sequence identifies continued left ventricular loading, rather than any residual valve lesion, as the reason resuscitation failed, and argues for anticipating unloading when extracorporeal support is instituted across a valve just rendered competent in a severely dysfunctional ventricle. The outcome appeared determined by end-organ injury already established before intervention.

title: Association of Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction with Left Atrial Remodeling and Dysfunction in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: A Three-Dimensional Echocardiography and Left Atrial Strain Study.
authors: Weili Lin; Runming Zhong; Qianqian Que; Wenwen Lin; Rui'e Zhu; Fulai Cai
abstract:
To compare left atrial (LA) structure and phasic function among healthy controls and patients with nonobstructive or obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), and assess their associations with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO).
We studied 90 patients with HCM and 50 healthy controls. Patients were classified by the highest resting or Valsalva-provoked LVOT gradient (LVOTG) as nonobstructive (<30 mmHg; n = 50) or obstructive (≥30 mmHg; n = 40). Threedimensional echocardiography measured LA volumes, and two-dimensional speckle tracking measured phasic strain. Multivariable linear regression examined prespecified echocardiographic outcomes by LVOTO status. Sensitivity analyses modeled LVOTG continuously and used a 50-mmHg threshold.
Both HCM groups had greater LA enlargement and dysfunction than controls, with the largest abnormalities in obstructive HCM. In the primary adjusted model, LVOTO was associated with higher LAVImin (B = 10.03 mL/m2; 95% CI, 6.71 to 13.36; p < 0.001) and lower LASr (B = -2.72%; 95% CI, -4.17 to -1.28; p < 0.001). The associations remained when LVOTG was analyzed per 10 mmHg and with a threshold of ≥50 mmHg. E/e' and TRV were not significantly associated with LVOTG in these sensitivity analyses.
In this cross-sectional HCM cohort, greater obstruction severity was associated with higher LAVImin and lower LASr. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether these measures are associated with clinical outcomes.

title: Valve-in-valve transcatheter mitral valve replacement via totally endoscopic endoclamp-assisted approach after failed bioprosthetic mitral valve: a case report.
authors: J Nader; A Roussiaux; J E Ricci; C Piot
abstract: Endoscopic Endoclampassisted MViV can expand the armamentarium for complex redo mitral surgery, offering excellent early clinical and haemodynamic results in selected patients. A 50 year-old man with heavy alcohol and tobacco use and two previous mitral operations (repair, then bioprosthetic replacement eight years earlier) presented with progressive dyspnoea (NYHA III). Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography revealed severe mixed stenosis/regurgitation of a 33 mm Medtronic Mosaic bioprothesis. No endocarditis was found preoperatively. After shared decisionmaking, minimally invasive videoassisted right minithoracotomy under endoaortic balloon occlusion (Endoclamp®) was planned. Intraoperatively, the degenerated valve was firmly embedded in the native annulus and could not be safely explanted. A 29 mm SAPIEN 3 Ultra transcatheter heart valve was therefore deployed inside the surgical frame under direct vision on cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Postdeployment echocardiography showed a mean gradient of 8 mmHg without paravalvular leak or LVOT compromise. The patient was extubated on postoperative day 2; aside from temporary difficulties in respiratory weaning, recovery was uneventful, and he was discharged home on day 9.

title: Anomalous papillary muscle insertion beyond hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: insights from reported cases.
authors: Yuki Kudo; Shinichiro Takahashi
abstract: Anomalous insertion of the papillary muscle (APM) into the mitral valve leaflet is a rare congenital abnormality of the subvalvular apparatus. Most published reports describe direct papillary muscle insertion in association with obstructive physiology, particularly in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), where it contributes to left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and systolic anterior motion (SAM)-related mitral regurgitation. However, similar papillary muscle-leaflet continuity may also serve as a primary mechanical determinant of valve dysfunction in patients without a clinical diagnosis of HCM. This review synthesizes published reports of APM insertion across different clinical contexts and interprets them within a mechanism-oriented framework based on LVOT dynamics and functional role of the papillary muscle rather than disease labels. Available reports indicate a heterogeneous clinical spectrum in which hemodynamic manifestations reflect interactions among papillary muscle anatomy, mitral valve mechanics, and ventricular geometry. Although LVOT obstruction remains an important presentation, many cases show predominant mitral regurgitation due to leaflet tethering or, less commonly, functional mitral stenosis from impaired diastolic leaflet opening. These phenotypes arise from subvalvular mechanical restriction rather than primary leaflet pathology. Echocardiography plays a central role in diagnosis, yet APM insertion may be overlooked if assessment focuses primarily on leaflet morphology or Doppler findings. Transesophageal echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging provide complementary anatomical detail for accurate characterization and surgical planning. Greater awareness of this geometry-based interaction and adoption of a structured imaging approach may reduce diagnostic oversight and improve decision-making in patients with atypical mitral valve dysfunction.

title: The predictive value of the hemodynamic profile for survival in patients undergoing transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair.
authors: Felix Ausbuettel; Fares Kano; Nikolaos Patsalis; Christin Fichera; Dimitar Divchev; Carlo-Federico Fichera
abstract:
Transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair (M-TEER) represents a safe treatment modality for patients with high-grade mitral regurgitation (MR). While clinical decision-making concerning the referral of suitable candidates for M-TEER is guided primarily by clinical and echocardiographic parameters, the potential of hemodynamic parameters obtained at the time of screening in predicting treatment outcomes has not been sufficiently investigated.
All patients who underwent M-TEER and who provided sufficient right heart catheterisation (RHC) data prior to M-TEER were enrolled for analysis. The investigated hemodynamic parameters were analysed descriptively and their associations with survival were estimated by univariable Cox regression analysis and Kaplan-Meier's analysis.
A total of 94 patients were analysed, of whom 92.6% (87/94) had concomitant pulmonary hypertension (PH). Analysis of the hemodynamic profile revealed that 46.8% (44/94) of patients had advanced-stage congestive heart failure with a cardiac index < 2 L/min/m2, and 68% (64/94) of patients had a cardiac power index <0.5 W/m2. According to the results of the Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses, a systolic pulmonary artery pressure (sPAP) > 60 mmHg and a mean right atrial pressure (RAP) > 20 mmHg were proven to be significant predictors of long-term survival after M-TEER.
Analysis of the hemodynamic profile, specifically the identified predictors, contributes to the improved identification of scenarios associated with a favourable prognosis in patients undergoing M-TEER.

title: Advantages and Limitations of the Use of Robots in Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Repair: Results From a Matched Direct Comparison.
authors: Kosuke Nakamae; Yoshitsugu Nakamura; Daiki Yoshiyama; Yuto Yasumoto; Miho Kuroda; Shintaro Sawa; Yuka Higuma; Kusumi Niitsuma; Masaki Ushijima; Akihiro Higashino; Yujiro Hayashi; Taisuke Nakayama; Hiroaki Yusa; Ryo Tsuruta; Yujiro Ito
abstract:
To compare the surgical outcomes of nonrobotic and robotic minimally invasive mitral valve repair.
We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent minimally invasive mitral valve repair from January 2014 to March 2024. After excluding the learning curve cases, early and midterm outcomes were compared.
A total of 422 patients who underwent minimally invasive mitral valve repair (nonrobotic, n = 103; robotic, n = 319) were enrolled. The robotic group had a higher EuroSCORE II (P < 0.001). After propensity matching, the final cohort included 84 and 168 patients in each group. In the robotic group after matching, concomitant procedures remained significantly more frequent (P = 0.030). However, operative time (P = 0.782) and cross-clamping time (P = 0.452) were comparable, whereas cardiopulmonary bypass time was significantly longer in the robotic group (P = 0.031). Postoperative blood transfusion (P < 0.001), chest tube output within 24 h (P < 0.001), and intensive care unit stay (P = 0.042) remained higher in the robotic group after matching. Postoperative mitral regurgitation was no greater than mild in both groups (P = 0.146). At 4 years, overall survival was 94.4% versus 98.4% (P = 0.215), and freedom from recurrence of moderate or greater mitral regurgitation was 98.5% versus 97.9% (P = 0.230) after matching. These results are consistent with those observed before matching.
Robotic mitral valve repair demonstrated comparable perioperative and midterm outcomes despite greater transfusion requirements and a higher frequency of concomitant procedures. The higher rate of concomitant procedures should be interpreted with caution because it may partly reflect differences in surgical era and patient selection.

title: PASCAL Precision System Outcomes by Implant Location and Lesion Location in Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation Patients From the STS/ACC TVT Registry.
authors: P Kasi Ramanathan; Raj Makkar; Thomas Waggoner; Azeem Latib; Robert M Kipperman; Ivan Hanson; Anjan K Sinha; Tarun Chakravarty; Rahul P Sharma; Jeremiah P Depta; Jorge A Castellanos; Susheel Kodali; Amar Krishnaswamy; Brian Whisenant; Daniel Menees; D Scott Lim; Fahad Gilani; Carlos E Sanchez; Neil Gheewala; Santiago Garcia; Hemal Gada; Samir Kapadia; Pinak B Shah; Brian Renard; Gus Theodos; Ricardo Yaryura; Blake Gardner; Daniel H Steinberg; Eric Gnall; Georges Kaddissi; Adnan K Chhatriwalla; Antonio H Frangieh; Mackram F Eleid; Philippe Géneréux; John T Saxon; Pedro Villablanca; Fadi Matar; Himanshu Agarwal; Stanley Chetcuti; Tiberio Frisoli; Firas Zahr
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract:
Mitral valve transcatheter edge-to-edge repair can be more challenging in noncentral regions of the valve and in anterior or bileaflet lesions. We assess effect of implant location and leaflet lesion location on safety and effectiveness of PASCAL Precision system in degenerative mitral regurgitation (MR).
Mitral valve transcatheter edge-to-edge repair outcomes in patients with degenerative MR treated with PASCAL Precision system (September 2022-October 2024), from the US STS/ACC TVT (Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology Transcatheter Valve Therapy) Registry, were analyzed by implant location (A2P2/non-A2P2) and leaflet lesion location (anterior/posterior/bileaflet). Procedural, clinical, and echocardiographic outcomes to 30 days were assessed.
At 30 days, both A2P2 (n=1526) and non-A2P2 (n=299) groups had low event rates (cardiovascular mortality: 1.1% versus 1.0%, mitral valve reintervention: 0.4% versus 0.0% and single leaflet device attachment: 0.5% versus 0.3%; all P>0.05) and demonstrated significant MR reduction (P<0.001 versus baseline) with no significant difference between groups (P=0.750) (MR ≤2+: 93.4% versus 95.4%; MR ≤1+: 72.0% versus 73.3%). Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary scores improved significantly in both groups (∆19.3, ∆17.7 points; P=0.741). The anterior (n=250), posterior (n=902), and bileaflet (n=192) disease groups also had low event rates (cardiovascular mortality: 0.4%, 1.1%, 0.0%; mitral valve reintervention: 0.8%, 0.1%, 0.5%; and single leaflet device attachment: 0.8%, 0.2%, 0.5%; all P>0.05), and demonstrated significant MR reduction (P<0.001 versus baseline) with no significant difference across groups (P=0.459) (MR ≤2+: 94.1%, 93.1%, and 94.5%; MR ≤1+: 79.0%, 69.2%, and 72.4%). All groups experienced significant improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary scores (∆21.4, ∆18.8, ∆12.0 points; P=0.087).
In real-world patients with degenerative mitral regurgitation, treatment with the PASCAL Precision system was associated with favorable safety and effectiveness at 30 days, regardless of implant location or leaflet lesion location.

title: Myocardial remodelling during sacubitril/valsartan therapy in patients with chronic heart failure.
authors: David Tabukashvili; Vera Kapetivadze; Tamar Lazashvili; Zviadi Maglaperidze
abstract: The aim of the study was to identify differences between aliskiren and sacubitril/valsartan in their ability to influence cardiac remodelling, metabolic balance, neurohumoral activation, and clinical symptom severity. A comparative assessment of the clinical effectiveness and impact on the structural and functional state of the myocardium was conducted for two therapeutic strategies in patients with chronic heart failure in Georgia over a 12-month follow-up. The results demonstrated fundamentally different trajectories of therapeutic response. In the sacubitril/valsartan group, early clinical improvement was observed by 6 months, including significant reductions in systolic blood pressure (-6.2%, p<0.001), respiratory rate (-4.5%, p<0.001), and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels (-10.0%, p<0.05), along with improved oxygen saturation (+3.5%, p<0.001). Left ventricular ejection fraction increased significantly already at 6 months (from 34.2±4.7% to 37.4±4.0%, p<0.001) and further at 12 months (40.5±3.5%, p<0.001), accompanied by rapid improvement in New York Heart Association functional class, with 9.3% of patients achieving New York Heart Association I by study end. In contrast, the aliskiren group exhibited slower but more pronounced structural reverse remodelling. Significant reductions in left ventricular end-systolic volume (-15.8%, p=0.009), end-diastolic volume (-17.6%, p=0.016), and end-systolic diameter (p=0.002) were observed only at 12 months, along with a modest but significant increase in ejection fraction (p=0.030). Regression of functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation and a significant decrease in pulmonary artery systolic pressure (-19.7%, p<0.05) were more prominent in this group. Both therapies led to significant improvements in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, including reductions in glycated haemoglobin, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides (p<0.05 for all), indicating a favourable systemic metabolic effect. Overall, findings suggest that sacubitril/valsartan may be preferable when rapid clinical stabilization is required, whereas aliskiren may represent an effective therapeutic option for patients with advanced structural cardiac remodelling.

title: Echocardiographic description of pulmonary vein stenosis in a cat with atrioventricular septal defect.
authors: Farzin Seyednejad; Laurent Locquet; Pantea Ardehali; Niusha Astaraki
abstract:
A 2.5-year-old, intact female British Shorthair cat was referred for cardiology evaluation owing to intermittent panting and a heart murmur identified on cardiac auscultation before elective surgery. Physical examination revealed a left parasternal grade II/VI systolic murmur without arrhythmia. Thoracic radiographs showed cardiomegaly without pulmonary infiltration. The echocardiography was prompted by auscultation, history and radiological findings. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated marked right atrial enlargement and eccentric hypertrophy of the right ventricle. Echocardiography revealed a partial atrioventricular septal defect characterised by a large ostium primum defect (0.79 cm) and an anterior mitral valve cleft, resulting in a left-to-right shunt (estimated Qp:Qs ≈ 2.2). Doppler interrogation of the left pulmonary vein entering the lateral wall of the left atrium demonstrated focal turbulence and increased peak velocity (1.08 m/s), corresponding to a pressure gradient of approximately 4.7 mmHg, findings consistent with suspected unilateral pulmonary vein stenosis. Tricuspid regurgitation velocity (2.2 m/s) did not reflect increased afterload. Elective surgery was postponed owing to uncertainty regarding peri-anaesthetic haemodynamic risk. Medical treatment with enalapril and clopidogrel was initiated. At the 9-month follow-up, the cat remained clinically stable and echocardiographic findings were unchanged.
Pulmonary vein stenosis is rarely reported in cats. This report describes the concurrent presence of partial atrioventricular septal defect and suspected unilateral pulmonary vein stenosis. These findings highlight the detection of a congenital heart defect in a young cat, despite the low-grade murmur.

title: Echocardiographic assessment of mitral regurgitation severity in dogs.
authors: L C Visser; B M Potter
journal: Journal of veterinary cardiology : the official journal of the European Society of Veterinary Cardiology
abstract: Mitral regurgitation (MR) is the most important cardiovascular problem affecting dogs. Transthoracic echocardiography is the most practical imaging modality to characterize the fundamental features of MR, including an assessment of MR severity. The diversity of MR severity in subclinical dogs and advancements in treatments directed at the cause of MR have (re)ignited interest in more comprehensive and quantitative methods of assessing MR severity. This review focuses on evaluating the severity of chronic MR in dogs. It discusses when a comprehensive assessment of MR severity is indicated. It highlights the strengths, limitations and challenges associated with the numerous structural, qualitative, semiquantitative and quantitative variables available to assess MR severity. The methods involved in determining the important quantitative variables of MR severity such as effective orifice area, regurgitant volume and regurgitant fraction are reviewed in detail. This paper advocates for an integrative approach, ideally from guidelines generated by an expert panel, where multiple echocardiographic variables from multiple categories are incorporated to assess MR severity and grade the MR as mild, moderate or severe. It summarizes the work on assessing MR severity in dogs to date and highlights shortcomings where there is much work to be done.

title: Mitral Annular Disjunction: Regional Strain Abnormalities Associated With Life-Threatening Ventricular Arrhythmias.
authors: Abdalaziz Awadelkarim; Jyothik Varun Inampudi; Farima Kahe; John Gallagher; Amanda Sandles; John Dawdy; Kendall Bell; Luis Afonso
abstract:
Mitral annular disjunction (MAD) has been linked to malignant ventricular arrhythmias in mitral valve prolapse, but the mechanisms and risk predictors are not well established. We aimed to identify clinical and echocardiographic factors with a focus on left ventricular (LV) strain.
We retrospectively studied 69 patients with MAD confirmed on echocardiogram. Clinical data and echocardiographic measurements were collected, including chamber dimensions, MAD distance, mitral regurgitation grade, and 2D global and segmental longitudinal strain by speckle-tracking. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to determine independent predictors of arrhythmia.
All patients had preserved LV ejection fraction. Patients with arrhythmias demonstrated trends toward larger chamber dimensions and a larger MAD distance. Global longitudinal strain did not significantly differ between groups. Differences between patients with and without life-threatening arrhythmias localized specifically to the inferolateral region at the mid-ventricular level, where mid-inferolateral strain was significantly worse in arrhythmic patients (median -12.6% [IQR 13.5] vs. -18.9% [IQR 6.0], p = 0.0069). In univariate models, factors associated with arrhythmias included larger LV chamber diameters, greater MAD distance, a history of syncope, and worse strain in the mid-inferior and mid-inferolateral segments. On exploratory multivariate analysis, mid-inferolateral strain impairment appears to be independently associated with LTA (OR 1.11 per 1% strain increase, p = 0.012).
In patients with MAD, impaired mid-inferolateral segment strain was associated with LTA, suggesting that regional myocardial deformation may provide incremental arrhythmic risk stratification beyond global measures. These findings are, however, exploratory, hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger, prospective cohorts with independent validation to ascertain clinical utility.

title: Trileaflet Mitral Valve as Unusual Contributor to Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authors: Nagarjuna Panidapu; Barsha Sen; Praveen Kerala Varma; Hisham Ahamed; Jes Jose; Don Jose Palamattam; Divya Mary Jacob; Thushara Madathil
abstract:
Mitral valve abnormalities are increasingly recognized as contributors to left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM). Although trileaflet mitral valves have been reported previously in patients with oHCM, this case demonstrates how detailed segmental echocardiographic phenotyping identified distinct mechanisms of dynamic LVOTO, enabling an individualized repair.
A 48-year-old man with oHCM was found to have a trileaflet mitral valve contributing to LVOTO in addition to systolic anterior motion.
Careful anatomical and functional assessment distinguished this anomaly from pseudo-trileaflet variants and enabled anatomy-directed repair while preserving the native valve.
In oHCM, comprehensive 2D and 3D imaging should define the mechanism of LVOTO and mitral regurgitation rather than simply identify anatomical abnormalities. Detailed mitral valve phenotyping can distinguish a true congenital trileaflet morphology from pseudo-trileaflet variants and reveal leaflet-specific mechanisms of obstruction. Mechanism-based imaging helps surgeons choose the most appropriate valve-preserving repair for each patient's valve abnormality.

title: Early outcomes of transcatheter vacuum-assisted mass extraction in the left heart and the aortic arch.
authors: Jonathan X Fang; Brian P O'Neill; Tiberio M Frisoli; Marvin H Eng; Pedro Engel Gonzalez; Junichi Shimamura; Hasan A Ahmad; Syed Abbas Haidry; Gennaro Giustino; Ahmad Jabri; Reda Ibrahim; Ralph Stephan von Bardeleben; Samuel Gregerson; Arturo Giacaman; Michael Chiang; Kent Chak-Yu So; Leo Kar Lok Lai; James C Lee; Bryan Zweig; Georgi K Fram; Dee Dee Wang; William W O'Neill; Pedro A Villablanca
journal: EuroIntervention : journal of EuroPCR in collaboration with the Working Group on Interventional Cardiology of the European Society of Cardiology
abstract:
Transcatheter vacuum-assisted mass extraction (TVME) in the systemic circulation is increasingly being reported. However, its feasibility, effectiveness, and safety remain poorly defined.
We sought to investigate the feasibility, effectiveness and safety of TVME in the left heart and aortic arch.
Consecutive patients from 6 centres in the United States and Canada were included. Feasibility was defined as technically successful mass extraction without unplanned cardiac surgery or intraprocedural mortality. The effectiveness endpoint was feasibility with successful debulking of ≥70% mass volume. The primary safety endpoint was the 30-day composite of procedure-attributable mortality, major cardiac structural complications, major vascular complications, Type 3-4 bleeding, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and stroke, all according to Valve Academic Research Consortium (VARC)-3 definitions. Intraprocedural events were also reported.
A total of 62 consecutive patients were evaluated. Feasibility was reached in 85.5% of patients and effectiveness in 77.4% of patients - except for 11.3% with suboptimal debulking, 3.2% with access-related case abortion, and 8.1% with case cancellation where no mass was found intraprocedurally. The primary safety endpoint occurred in 14.5% of patients, with a procedure-attributable mortality rate of 3.2%. VARC-3 major cardiac structural complications, major vascular complications, Type 3-4 bleeding, ACS, and stroke occurred in 3.2%, 8.1%, 3.2%, 3.2%, and 6.5% of patients, respectively. Intraprocedural events included hypoxia (6.5%), hypotension (9.7%), embolism (3.2%), air embolism (1.6%), and increased mitral regurgitation (6.5%).
TVME in left-sided and aortic arch masses is feasible and demonstrates reasonable effectiveness. However, the considerable rate of safety-related events highlights the need for better case selection and procedural refinement, such as optimal embolic protection.

title: Determining the Optimal Treatment Strategy for Patients With Combined Aortic Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation.
authors: Grant W Reed; Eric D Warner

title: A Whole-Heart Fluid-Structure Interaction Model for Transcatheter Mitral Valve Repair in Primary Mitral Regurgitation.
authors: Masod Sadipour; Marshall Davey; David R Wells; Arash Kheradvar; John P Vavalle; Boyce E Griffith
abstract:
Primary mitral regurgitation (MR) resulting from chordal rupture leads to acute volume overload and elevated left atrial pressure. Transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair (TMVr) devices can effectively reduce MR, but their impact on global cardiac mechanics and diastolic filling remains difficult to predict. This study develops a whole-heart FSI framework for TMVr by extending a previously developed whole-heart model to represent chordal rupture and edge-to-edge repair and to quantify their structural and hemodynamic consequences.
A three-dimensional FSI model of the heart derived from cardiac CT imaging was used to simulate three conditions: healthy baseline, chordal rupture-induced MR, and post-TMVr. The immersed finite element-difference method enables fully coupled simulation of blood flow, valve dynamics, and myocardial contraction. Hemodynamic metrics, including regurgitant fraction (RF), left atrial pressure (LAP), stroke volume (SV), stroke work (SW), and pressure-volume relationships, were compared with clinical reference data.
Chordal rupture produced moderate-to-severe MR (RF = 38%) and doubled left atrial V-wave amplitude, consistent with clinical observations. After TMVr, the central regurgitant jet produced by chordal rupture was eliminated, RF decreased to 21%, and LAP returned to near-baseline levels. However, the double-orifice valve configuration generated dual high-velocity inflow jets and reduced diastolic filling.
The repair effectively reduces regurgitation and atrial pressure while also influencing diastolic filling and ventricular output. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating both regurgitation reduction and inflow characteristics when assessing TMVr outcomes and demonstrate the potential of patient-specific computational modeling for procedural planning and optimization.

title: [Evidence-based treatment of valvular heart disease].
authors: Felix S Nettersheim; Stephan Baldus
abstract: Valvular heart disease is a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality worldwide. As the prevalence of most valvular heart diseases increases with age, population ageing has led to a substantial increase in disease burden. Due to advanced age or significant comorbidities, many patients are considered unsuitable for conventional surgery. Whereas medical therapy was therefore often the only treatment option in the past, the rapid evolution of transcatheter interventions has fundamentally transformed the management of valvular heart disease over the past two decades. Today, effective catheter-based treatment options are available for virtually all valvular pathologies. For patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis, the prognostic benefit of transcatheter aortic valve replacement is firmly established. Large randomized trials have demonstrated non-inferiority of transcatheter aortic valve replacement compared with surgical aortic valve replacement across most patient populations, leading to an expanding use of this approach in younger and lower-risk patients. Similarly, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair for mitral and tricuspid regurgitation has been shown to improve symptoms, quality of life, and heart failure-related hospitalizations. In carefully selected patients with secondary mitral regurgitation, this strategy also confers a survival benefit. In addition, dedicated transcatheter devices have recently emerged as promising treatment options for native aortic regurgitation. Given the rapid evolution of transcatheter therapies, current efforts are increasingly focused on selecting the optimal treatment strategy for the individual patient and determining the optimal timing of intervention.

title: Overcoming Treatment Inertia for Mitral Transcatheter Edge-To-Edge Repair: Wait No Longer.
authors: Yinghao Lim; Anne Tay; Edgar Tay

title: Acute Mitral Regurgitation With Unilateral Pulmonary Edema: Preferential Pulmonary Venous Loading From an Eccentric Jet.
authors: Kevin Zhang; Mark Ishak; Mathew Doyle; Melissa Baraket; Craig Juergens
abstract:
Acute severe mitral regurgitation (MR) can cause rapidly progressive asymmetric pulmonary edema that mimics pneumonia.
A 22-year-old man presented with fever, dyspnea, and a new pansystolic murmur. Within hours, he developed hypoxemic respiratory failure. Serial chest imaging captured rapid progression from subtle right hilar vascular prominence to extensive right-predominant airspace opacification. Echocardiography showed posterior leaflet chordal rupture with a flail P2 segment and a severe eccentric MR jet directed toward the right pulmonary venous inflow, with systolic flow reversal in a sampled right pulmonary vein. Mitral valve repair produced marked clinical and radiographic improvement.
Concordance among the MR jet trajectory, pulmonary venous abnormalities, and edema distribution supported preferential right pulmonary venous loading. Recognition of this pattern helped distinguish asymmetric cardiogenic pulmonary edema from pneumonia.
Rapidly evolving focal pulmonary opacification with a new systolic murmur should prompt urgent echocardiography.

title: First Experience of a New Transfemoral Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement System.
authors: Christian Frerker; Christoph Marquetand; Francesco Bedogni; Jonathan Byrne; Rodrigo Estévez-Loureiro; Marino Labinaz; Scott D Lim; Bruno Melica; Ingo Eitel; Tobias Schmidt

title: Ventricular arrhythmic burden before and after mitral valve repair in mitral valve prolapse: the role of mitral annular disjunction.
authors: Ümeyir Savur; Berhan Keskin; Aysel Akhundova; Aykun Hakgor; Bilal Boztosun
abstract:
Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) is increasingly recognized as an arrhythmogenic condition, with a subset of patients exhibiting ventricular arrhythmias beyond the hemodynamic effects of mitral regurgitation (MR). Mitral annular disjunction (MAD) has been proposed as a structural marker associated with arrhythmic risk, but its relationship with postoperative ventricular arrhythmias after mitral valve repair remains incompletely understood. We aimed to evaluate changes in ventricular arrhythmic burden following mitral valve repair and to investigate the association between preoperative MAD and postoperative ventricular ectopy.
This retrospective observational study included 77 patients with MVP who underwent surgical mitral valve repair for severe MR and had both preoperative and postoperative 24-h Holter recordings. Premature ventricular complex (PVC) burden and ventricular arrhythmias were assessed before and after surgery. MAD was evaluated retrospectively using transthoracic echocardiography. Multivariable linear regression, sensitivity analyses, and sequential model comparison were performed to evaluate the independent and incremental association of MAD with postoperative PVC burden.
Overall PVC burden decreased significantly after mitral valve repair. Patients with preoperative MAD had a substantially higher PVC burden both before surgery [7,800 (7,000-9,575) vs. 4,200 (3,200-6,200) PVCs/24 h, p < 0.001] and after surgery [5,700 (5,175-6,425) vs. 2,200 (1,800-3,500) PVCs/24 h, p < 0.001] than those without MAD. The relative reduction in PVC burden was comparable between groups (-35.4 ± 20.6% vs. -39.5 ± 29.5%, p = 0.113). In multivariable analysis, preoperative MAD remained independently associated with higher postoperative PVC burden after adjustment for clinical covariates, prolapse phenotype, residual mitral regurgitation, and baseline PVC burden.
Mitral valve repair was associated with a significant reduction in ventricular ectopic burden in patients with MVP. However, preoperative MAD identified patients with a higher postoperative ventricular ectopic burden despite a similar proportional reduction in PVCs. These findings support the potential value of postoperative rhythm surveillance in patients with preoperative MAD.

title: Severe continuous prosthetic mitral regurgitation from chordal rupture after valve-sparing replacement: a case report.
authors: Hongxia Wang; Yun Mou; Jiabin Yuan
abstract:
After mitral valve replacement with preservation of the subvalvular apparatus, prosthetic dysfunction resulting from retained native structures is extremely rare. When it occurs, it may directly threaten the patient's life. We report an unusual case of severe regurgitation resulting from preserved chordal rupture. The key distinction of this case is the presentation of late, severe continuous prosthetic regurgitation and reversibility.
A 54-year-old man had undergone double mechanical valve replacement for severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with mild regurgitation and concomitant aortic regurgitation three years earlier. During surgery, the posterior mitral leaflet and its entire subvalvular apparatus were preserved. Current transesophageal echocardiography revealed a mobile, cord-like structure between the lateral occluder and the prosthetic sewing ring, interfering with leaflet excursion and preventing full closure. This was accompanied by severe prosthetic mitral continuous regurgitation. Surgical findings revealed a ruptured chordae tendineae at the papillary muscle attachment, with the remnant preventing leaflet coaptation. Surgical excision of the ruptured chordal remnant successfully restored normal leaflet function, with complete resolution of the regurgitation confirmed on intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography.
When obstruction or regurgitation develops after valve replacement with subvalvular preservation, uncommon causes-such as residual subvalvular tissue or ruptured chordal entrapment-should be considered after excluding more common etiologies. This case illustrates the critical role of transesophageal echocardiography in the diagnosis of chordal entrapment after mitral valve replacement and potentially in preventing complications. The potential benefit of preserving the subvalvular apparatus warrants thoughtful deliberation. Surgical removal of the offending tissue or valve replacement remains the definitive treatment.

title: [Midterm outcomes of transcatheter edge-to-edge repair mitral valve guided solely by transesophageal echocardiography].
authors: W Z Xing; Y Han; Y H Zhang; G Han; Z R Sun; L L Ben; S B Song; Z B Lang; G J Zhang; X B Pan; Y Han
journal: Zhonghua xin xue guan bing za zhi
abstract: Objective: To preliminarily evaluate the efficacy and safety of transcatheter edge-to-edge repair of the mitral valve (MV-TEER) guided solely by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Methods: A total of 46 patients with mitral regurgitation who underwent MV-TEER guided solely by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) at Central China Fuwai Hospital of Zhengzhou University from January 2023 to January 2024 were retrospectively enrolled. Follow-up was performed at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after the procedure, including echocardiography, 6-minute walk test, New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification, and grading of mitral regurgitation severity. Hospitalization for heart failure, repeat mitral valve intervention, and all-cause mortality were recorded. The cumulative incidence of rehospitalization for heart failure was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Results: The median age of the enrolled patients was 67.5 (59.0, 73.0) years, and 29 patients (63%) were male. MV-TEER was successfully performed under sole TEE guidance in all 46 patients. The median follow-up duration was 15.80 (12.63, 20.64) months. The 1-year rehospitalization rate for heart failure was 20%, and 1 patient died of malignant arrhythmia. There was no repeat mitral valve intervention. At 1 year after the procedure, the left ventricular end-systolic diameter decreased significantly from (47.17±11.31) mm to (39.71±7.44) mm (P<0.05). The left ventricular end-systolic volume decreased from (87.02±20.63) ml to (72.18±17.30) ml (P<0.05), and the left ventricular ejection fraction improved from (44.98±11.78)% to (51.84±10.03)% (P<0.05). Five patients had mitral regurgitation grade 3+, while the remaining patients had grade less than 3+. Three patients were in NYHA functional class Ⅲ, 23 in class Ⅱ, and 19 in class Ⅰ. The 6-minute walk distance improved significantly from (298±78) m to (375±70) m (P<0.05). Conclusion: It is preliminarily demonstrated that MV-TEER guided solely by TEE is safe and effective, and patients have favorable midterm outcomes.

authors: Katane Elizabeth Kekana; Thokozani Isaac Mtshali

abstract: Teaching learners with special educational needs requires dynamic and adaptive pedagogical strategies that can lead to social development and academic success. This can be possible if teachers are assisted in mitigating the daily challenges of teaching such learners. This qualitative exploratory case study investigated the pedagogical challenges encountered by two Grade 9 Technology teachers in the Capricorn District of Limpopo Province. This study used Shulman’s Content and Pedagogical Knowledge framework to understand teachers’ challenges. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews and classroom observations; all collected data were analysed thematically. This study found that teachers experienced various challenges, including the emotional labour of teaching, burnout in the LSEN environment and the enactment of instructional knowledge. The study concluded that the sampled teachers displayed weaknesses in lesson planning, activating learners’ prior knowledge, diagnosing errors, achieving curriculum objectives and sustaining engagement. As a result, it was recommended that support through teacher assistants, creative differentiated strategies and enhanced digital-technology literacy to improve outcomes for learners with special needs was imminent.
